tasks.prompt: Your school is discussing how social media and advertising affect students' body image. Write a text for the school community in which you explain the problem, suggest practical ways the school can respond, and persuade students to value a broader idea of confidence and self-worth.
requirements: Explain how unrealistic beauty standards can affect students.
Suggest practical actions the school community can take.
Persuade the audience to value qualities beyond appearance.
tasks.audience: Students and the wider school community
tasks.purpose: Raise awareness and persuade readers to support a healthier view of beauty and self-worth
tasks.textTypeRationale: An opinion column is best because the task asks for explanation plus a clear personal position aimed at a broad school audience.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: 問題提起→具体策→反論への対応→結論という流れで、Criterion Bの展開と一貫性を作っています。Opinion columnとして読者に直接働きかける声と明確な立場を保っている点がCriterion C対策です。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Why We Need a Healthier Idea of Beauty

Every morning, many students open social media before they even get out of bed. Within minutes, they see carefully edited photographs, advertisements for “perfect” bodies and videos that suggest confidence can be bought with the right product. It is easy to dismiss this as harmless entertainment, but the effect on teenagers’ self-image can be serious.

Our school can help by changing the conversation. First, we should teach students how images are created. Filters, lighting, selective editing and paid promotion can make ordinary people look unrealistically flawless. When students understand these techniques, they are less likely to compare themselves with an artificial standard. Media literacy should therefore be discussed not only in technology lessons but also in health and advisory classes.

Second, we need to make diversity visible. School posters, newsletters and events should represent different body types, cultures, abilities and styles instead of repeating one narrow image of attractiveness. This does not mean telling everyone to ignore appearance. It means recognizing that appearance is only one part of identity and that no single body shape deserves to be treated as the standard.

Finally, students themselves should be part of the solution. A student-led campaign could invite people to share short messages about qualities they value in themselves that have nothing to do with appearance: kindness, persistence, creativity, humour or courage. Peer support is especially important because teenagers often listen more closely to one another than to adults.

Some people may argue that schools already have too many responsibilities and that beauty standards are a private issue. However, when unrealistic expectations affect concentration, confidence, relationships and mental health, they become an educational issue as well. Schools cannot control every image students see, but they can give us the tools to respond critically.

Parents and teachers can support the same message by changing the way compliments are used. If young people hear praise only for being thin, fashionable or attractive, appearance becomes a measure of worth even when adults do not intend that. Praising effort, imagination, reliability and empathy gives students a broader picture of success. This is not about banning discussion of looks; it is about making sure that appearance is not the loudest message.

Schools could also review dress-code language so that rules focus on safety and learning rather than shaming particular bodies or styles.

A healthier idea of beauty will not be created by one assembly or one poster. It will grow when students repeatedly hear that their value is not measured by likes, clothing size or resemblance to an influencer. If our school wants young people to become confident and independent thinkers, helping them question unrealistic beauty standards is a practical place to start.

tasks.prompt: Your school is preparing rules for the use of generative AI in learning. Write a text for school leaders in which you identify benefits and risks, recommend clear rules for students and teachers, and explain how the policy should be introduced and reviewed.
requirements: Identify educational benefits and risks of generative AI.
Recommend clear rules for acceptable use.
Explain how the policy should be introduced and reviewed.
tasks.purpose: Recommend a practical and balanced school AI policy
tasks.textTypeRationale: A proposal naturally organizes recommendations, implementation and expected benefits for decision-makers.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: 見出しを使い、現状→推奨策→導入→利点→結論と整理したProposalです。Audienceが学校管理者なので、感情的にならず実行可能性を重視したformal registerにしています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Proposal: Responsible Use of Generative AI at Our School

Purpose
This proposal recommends a school policy that allows students to use generative artificial intelligence as a learning tool while protecting academic honesty, privacy and independent thinking.

Current situation
Students are already using AI tools to explain difficult concepts, generate practice questions and improve drafts. Banning the technology completely would be difficult to enforce and would ignore its educational value. At the same time, unrestricted use creates genuine problems. Students may submit work they did not produce, accept inaccurate information without checking it, or enter private data into external systems.

Recommended policy
First, the school should define acceptable and unacceptable uses. Acceptable uses could include brainstorming, receiving feedback on grammar, creating revision quizzes and asking for explanations of material already taught. Unacceptable uses should include submitting AI-generated writing as original work, using AI during assessments unless specifically permitted, and asking a system to complete tasks designed to demonstrate personal understanding.

Second, students should disclose significant AI assistance. A short statement such as “AI was used to generate practice questions and check sentence clarity” would encourage transparency without treating all use as misconduct. Teachers could also specify different rules for different assignments.

Third, the school should teach verification skills. AI can produce confident but incorrect answers, so students need to compare claims with reliable sources. Lessons should also explain bias, copyright and the risks of uploading names, photographs or confidential school information.

The policy should also protect teacher judgment. Different subjects use AI in different ways, so one rule cannot cover every situation. A design class might permit image generation for brainstorming, while a language assessment may require entirely independent writing. Teachers should therefore state the permitted level of assistance when setting work, and students should be able to ask questions before submission rather than discovering the rule only after a problem occurs.

Implementation
The policy should begin with a one-term trial. Teachers from several subjects could record common problems and successful uses, while students could complete a short survey about whether the rules are clear. The policy could then be revised before becoming permanent.

Expected benefits
A balanced approach would prepare students for a world in which AI is increasingly common while still protecting the purpose of education. Students would learn not only how to use powerful technology but when not to use it. Teachers would gain clearer expectations, and disagreements about academic honesty would be reduced.

Conclusion
The school should not choose between unlimited AI use and a total ban. It should create transparent boundaries, require responsible disclosure and explicitly teach verification and privacy. Such a policy would support innovation without allowing technology to replace the thinking that students are here to develop.

tasks.prompt: After another severe summer heatwave, your city council is asking residents for views on local climate action. Write a text in which you argue for specific local measures, address concerns about cost or effectiveness, and explain why action at city level matters.
requirements: Recommend specific local climate measures.
Address concerns about cost or effectiveness.
Explain why city-level action matters.
tasks.purpose: Persuade the community and council to support practical local climate action
tasks.textTypeRationale: A letter to the editor suits a public argument responding to a local issue and allows a clear persuasive position.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: 地域の読者に向けて、緑化・建物・交通・緊急情報など具体策を提示しています。反論も扱うことでMessageを深め、letter to the editorらしいpublic-facingなtoneを維持しています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Dear Editor,

Last summer our city experienced another period of extreme heat, yet public discussion quickly moved on once temperatures fell. That is a mistake. Heatwaves are not only uncomfortable days; they expose weaknesses in housing, transport, health services and the way our neighbourhoods are designed. Local climate action should therefore become a practical priority rather than an occasional slogan.

The first step is to cool the places where people actually live. Trees, shaded bus stops and small green spaces can reduce local temperatures while making streets more pleasant to walk through. The city should prioritize areas with little existing shade, especially neighbourhoods where residents are less able to afford air conditioning. Climate policy should not create a situation in which protection depends on personal income.

Buildings also matter. Better insulation, reflective roofs and efficient cooling systems can reduce indoor heat and electricity demand at the same time. The council could offer grants for older homes, schools and care facilities, beginning with buildings used by vulnerable people. Such measures cost money, but repeated emergency responses and rising energy demand also have a cost.

Transport is another important part of the solution. If buses are unreliable or cycling feels dangerous, residents will continue to depend on private cars. More frequent public transport, safe cycling routes and walkable streets would reduce emissions and give people realistic alternatives. These changes should be designed with residents rather than imposed without consultation.

Of course, one city cannot stop global climate change by itself. Critics may say that local action is insignificant compared with national energy policy or emissions from large industries. However, that argument confuses scale with responsibility. Local governments control planning, public space, transport and many public buildings. They can also demonstrate solutions that other communities may copy.

Preparation should also include clear communication during heat emergencies. Residents need to know where cooling centres are, how to check on vulnerable neighbours and when schools or outdoor events will change schedules. Information should be available in the main languages used locally and distributed through community groups, not only on a council website. Adaptation fails if the people at greatest risk do not receive the information in a form they can use.

Businesses and schools should be included as partners as well. Employers can adjust outdoor working hours during severe heat, while schools can expand shaded areas and review sports schedules. Shared responsibility will make city plans more effective than expecting individual residents to solve the problem alone.

We should judge climate action by whether it improves daily life as well as lowering long-term risk. A shaded street, an efficient home and a dependable bus service are useful even before their climate benefits are counted. The recent heatwave showed us what inaction looks like. The council now has an opportunity to show what serious preparation looks like.

Yours faithfully,
A concerned resident

tasks.prompt: You spent part of your holiday volunteering with a community food programme. The experience challenged some of your assumptions about poverty and volunteering. Write a text in which you describe what happened, explain how your perspective changed, and reflect on what meaningful volunteering requires.
requirements: Describe key aspects of the volunteering experience.
Explain how your assumptions changed.
Reflect on what meaningful volunteering requires.
tasks.audience: Peers and general readers interested in personal experiences
tasks.purpose: Reflect on a meaningful experience and share a changed perspective
tasks.textTypeRationale: A blog allows a personal voice, reflection and direct engagement with readers while still developing ideas in depth.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: 体験の描写だけで終わらず、自分の思い込みがどう変わったかを中心にしています。Blogらしいpersonal voiceを保ちながら、reflectionを深めることでCriterion BとCを両立させています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
What a Week of Volunteering Changed for Me

I joined a community food programme during the school holiday because I wanted to do something “useful.” I imagined that I would spend a week packing boxes, feel good about helping and then return to normal life. Instead, the experience changed the way I think about both volunteering and poverty.

On the first day, I was surprised by how organized the programme was. Donations had to be checked, sorted and matched with different household needs. Volunteers also prepared information about local services and helped elderly residents carry food home. I had assumed that helping was mainly about generosity, but I soon understood that good intentions are not enough. Reliable systems, respectful communication and local knowledge matter just as much.

The biggest change came from speaking with people who used the service. Before volunteering, I had unconsciously imagined poverty as something distant and obvious. In reality, some visitors were working, studying or caring for relatives. A sudden rent increase, illness or loss of hours at work had simply made their budgets impossible. Their experiences challenged the easy stereotype that people only need help because they have made poor choices.

I also became more aware of dignity. Volunteers were told not to speak about “giving to the needy” in front of visitors. Instead, people chose items in a shop-like space whenever possible. That small difference mattered. Assistance should not require someone to surrender their privacy or self-respect.

Another lesson was how easy it is for volunteers to centre their own feelings. At first I noticed whether I felt useful, tired or proud. Gradually I learned to ask a better question: did the service actually make things easier for the people using it? That shift sounds obvious, but it changes behaviour. It means listening to feedback, doing routine jobs well and accepting that the most visible task is not always the most important one.

The week did not turn me into an expert on inequality. In fact, it made me more cautious about claiming simple solutions. Food support can help families immediately, but it does not solve high housing costs, insecure work or unequal access to healthcare. Volunteering is valuable, yet it should not become an excuse for ignoring larger social problems.

Since returning to school, I have continued volunteering twice a month, but my motivation is different. I no longer see myself as someone arriving to “save” other people. I see the programme as a community in which everyone contributes different things at different times.

Travel is often described as an experience that changes your perspective. I did not travel far at all. I took a twenty-minute bus ride across town. That was enough to discover how limited my assumptions had been, and that may be the most valuable journey I made all year.

tasks.prompt: A public debate in your region questions whether minority languages should receive greater support in schools. Write a text in which you discuss benefits and challenges, consider the need for a shared language, and present your view on how schools should respond.
requirements: Discuss benefits of minority-language education.
Acknowledge practical challenges and the need for a shared language.
Present a balanced and clear position.
tasks.audience: Members of the public interested in education policy
tasks.purpose: Present a reasoned position in a public debate
tasks.textTypeRationale: An opinion column is designed for public argument and allows the writer to weigh competing considerations before reaching a position.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: 一方的に賛成するのではなく、共通言語の必要性や実施上の制約も扱っています。Public debate向けのopinion columnとして、balanced argumentを作ることが高得点のポイントです。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Why Minority Languages Belong in Education

When schools decide which languages deserve classroom time, they are making more than a practical timetable choice. They are also sending a message about whose identity, history and knowledge are considered valuable. For that reason, minority-language education should be seen as an educational opportunity rather than an obstacle to national unity.

Supporters of one dominant school language often make a reasonable point: students need a shared language to participate fully in higher education, employment and public life. A school system that fails to teach that language well can unintentionally limit students’ opportunities. However, this does not require schools to erase the languages children already speak.

Bilingual and minority-language programmes can strengthen belonging. When students see their home language used in books, school events or selected lessons, they receive a clear signal that their background is not something to hide. Families may also participate more confidently when schools communicate in languages they understand. This can build trust between institutions and communities.

There are academic benefits as well. Learning through more than one language encourages students to compare vocabulary, meaning and cultural perspectives. It can make them more conscious of how language shapes communication. The aim should not be to isolate students inside one linguistic community, but to help them become confident users of both a shared public language and their heritage language.

Minority languages can also preserve knowledge that is difficult to translate perfectly. Stories, local place names, oral histories and traditional environmental knowledge often carry meanings connected to a particular language. When a language disappears from education, students may lose access not only to words but to ways of describing experience. Schools do not need to romanticize every tradition, but they should recognize that language can be an academic and cultural resource.

Implementation, of course, is difficult. Schools need trained teachers, suitable materials and enough students to make programmes sustainable. In areas with many small language groups, offering full bilingual instruction in every language may be impossible. Flexible approaches are therefore necessary: optional classes, bilingual resources, community partnerships and after-school programmes can all contribute.

The most important principle is that integration should not be confused with assimilation. Students can learn the language of the wider society without being asked to abandon another part of themselves. A strong education system should expand a young person’s ability to communicate, not replace one identity with another.

Minority-language education will look different in different regions, and no single model will suit every school. Nevertheless, treating linguistic diversity as a resource rather than a problem creates a better starting point. Schools prepare students for society. In a multilingual society, learning to respect and navigate more than one language is not a distraction from that purpose; it is part of it.

tasks.prompt: Your student council wants to improve the way new international students are welcomed. Write a text to students in which you explain why diversity alone does not guarantee belonging, propose practical improvements, and encourage students to take responsibility for creating an intercultural community.
requirements: Explain why diversity alone does not guarantee inclusion.
Propose practical improvements for welcoming new students.
Motivate students to take personal responsibility.
tasks.purpose: Motivate peers to build a more genuinely intercultural school community
tasks.textTypeRationale: A speech is best for motivating a student audience and allows direct address, repetition and a strong call to action.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: Speechとして冒頭で問題を提示し、3つの具体策を分かりやすく展開しています。最後にstudent councilへの行動提案を置き、audienceへの直接的なcall to actionにつなげています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Good morning everyone,

When new students arrive at an international school, we often say, “You’ll fit in quickly.” We mean to be encouraging, but fitting in is not automatic. A school can contain dozens of nationalities and still leave some people feeling invisible. Today I want to suggest three simple ways we can make our welcome more genuinely intercultural.

First, we need to move beyond the idea that culture means food, flags and festivals. Those things can be enjoyable, but they are only the surface. Culture also affects humour, classroom participation, attitudes to time, family expectations and the way people show disagreement. Instead of asking new students only where they are from, we should create opportunities to hear how they experience school and what feels unfamiliar.

Second, every new student should have a peer contact for the first month. This should not be a “tour guide” who disappears after one day. A peer contact could explain small things that teachers may never think to mention: where students sit at lunch, how clubs work, which online systems matter and what to do when you do not understand an informal expression. These details can determine whether someone feels confident enough to join in.

Third, intercultural welcome has to work both ways. New students should not carry the entire responsibility for adapting. Current students can learn to pronounce unfamiliar names, avoid jokes based on stereotypes and ask questions without treating someone as a representative of an entire country. Curiosity is valuable, but respect matters more than collecting interesting facts about other people.

Teachers can support this effort too. A new student may understand a subject well but need extra time to process instructions in English, while another may speak fluently but still find classroom expectations unfamiliar. Avoiding assumptions is crucial. Asking what kind of support helps is more respectful than deciding in advance what someone needs. A welcoming school should be flexible enough to notice these differences without making students feel singled out.

Some of us may think this is unnecessary because our school is already diverse. But diversity describes who is present; inclusion describes what happens after people arrive. A multicultural student body is not automatically an intercultural community.

I would like the student council to create a small welcome team next term, with volunteers from different year groups. We could organize peer contacts, gather anonymous feedback from newcomers and produce a short “things I wish I had known” guide written by students themselves.

Belonging is built through repeated, ordinary interactions. A greeting, an invitation to sit together, a correctly pronounced name or a patient explanation can matter more than a large international festival once a year. Let us become a school that does not merely include many cultures in its statistics, but learns how to live well across them.

Thank you.

tasks.prompt: A youth magazine is publishing views on how recommendation algorithms affect friendships and social behaviour. Write a text in which you explain possible effects on attention and opinions, acknowledge benefits of social media, and argue what users or platforms should do differently.
requirements: Explain how recommendation algorithms may affect behaviour or relationships.
Acknowledge benefits of social media.
Argue for practical changes by users or platforms.
tasks.audience: Teenage and young adult magazine readers
tasks.purpose: Encourage critical thinking about algorithm-driven social media
tasks.textTypeRationale: An opinion column supports a clear viewpoint while allowing explanation, counterargument and direct engagement with a general readership.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: アルゴリズムを単純な悪者にせず、利点も認めた上で問題点を評価しています。Counterargumentを入れながら最終的な立場を明確にすることで、Messageの深さを出しています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
The Algorithm Is Not a Friend

Social media platforms often describe their recommendation systems as tools that help users “discover what they love.” That sounds harmless. Yet an algorithm does not know us in the way a friend does. It measures what keeps us watching, clicking and returning. When that goal shapes our information environment, the effect on relationships deserves more attention.

The first problem is attention. A conversation with another person develops slowly and includes pauses, uncertainty and compromise. A personalized feed offers the opposite: endless novelty with almost no effort. If every spare moment is filled by content selected to hold our attention, ordinary conversation can begin to feel less stimulating. The result is not necessarily that technology makes people antisocial, but that it trains us to expect constant reward.

Algorithms can also narrow what we see. If a user repeatedly watches one type of political or cultural content, the platform may provide more of the same. This can create the impression that “everyone sensible agrees with me,” even when society is far more diverse. Friends who hold different opinions may then seem not merely different but irrational or threatening. Online personalization can therefore make face-to-face disagreement harder.

There is another issue: comparison. Recommendation systems learn which images attract engagement, and extreme or highly polished content often performs well. Teenagers may repeatedly see lifestyles, bodies or achievements that are unusual but presented as normal. That can create insecurity and competition even among close friends.

There is also a business reason to be cautious. Platforms earn money from attention, so their interests do not always match ours. A recommendation system may keep showing emotionally intense content because outrage, fear or envy increase engagement. That does not mean companies deliberately want users to be unhappy, but it does mean we should question a design in which longer screen time is automatically treated as success. Human wellbeing needs a different measurement.

However, blaming algorithms for every problem would be too simple. Social media also helps people maintain long-distance friendships, find communities and discover perspectives they would never meet locally. Users are not powerless either. We can choose whom to follow, turn off notifications and leave platforms that damage our wellbeing.

The better response is greater transparency and digital literacy. Platforms should explain why content is recommended and give users meaningful control over their feeds. Schools should teach students to recognize how engagement-based systems influence attention and emotion.

Technology does not eliminate human choice, but it can shape the environment in which choices are made. An algorithm may be useful, entertaining and sometimes surprisingly accurate. We should simply stop confusing accurate prediction of our clicks with genuine understanding of our lives. Friendship requires attention to another person; a platform requires attention from us. Those are not the same relationship.

tasks.prompt: Your school canteen wants student proposals for reducing food waste. Write a text in which you explain the causes of current waste, recommend several practical measures, and describe how the school should measure whether the plan succeeds.
requirements: Explain likely causes of school food waste.
Recommend several practical measures.
Describe how success should be measured.
tasks.purpose: Recommend an implementable food-waste reduction programme
tasks.textTypeRationale: A proposal is designed to present a problem, recommendations, implementation and evaluation to decision-makers.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: ProposalのconventionsとしてAim/Problem/Recommended actions/Evaluation/Conclusionを使用しています。単なる環境意識ではなく、測定・試行・評価まで示すことでtask fulfillmentを高めています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Proposal: Cutting Food Waste at School

Aim
This proposal recommends a practical programme to reduce food waste in the school canteen while maintaining student choice and avoiding unnecessary additional costs.

Problem
Large amounts of edible food are thrown away after lunch each day. Some waste comes from portions that are too large, while some results from students taking items they do not want because meals are sold as fixed combinations. Food waste represents wasted money, energy, water and transport, and it also increases the amount of rubbish the school must manage.

Recommended actions
1. Measure before acting. For two weeks, canteen staff and student volunteers should separate unavoidable waste, such as fruit peels, from edible leftovers. Recording which dishes are most often discarded will allow the school to target the real causes rather than relying on guesses.

2. Offer flexible portions. Students could choose regular or small portions for selected meals, with the option to return for more where practical. This would be especially useful for rice, pasta and side dishes. Smaller default portions do not have to mean less food; they mean less food placed on a tray before a student knows how much they need.

3. Improve choice. If fixed meal sets cause unwanted items to be discarded, students should be able to exchange one side dish for another. A simple pre-order system for popular meals could also help the kitchen estimate demand more accurately.

4. Share results. A monthly display could show how many kilograms of edible food were wasted and whether the figure is falling. The message should avoid blaming individual students and instead emphasize collective progress.

5. Deal responsibly with unavoidable waste. Where local rules permit, food that cannot be served safely should be composted rather than sent to general waste.

The canteen should also consider communication. If students do not understand why changes are being made, smaller portions may be interpreted simply as a cost-cutting exercise. A short explanation at the start of the trial should make clear that students can request more food and that the aim is to reduce what is discarded, not what is eaten. Transparency will make cooperation more likely and will help distinguish genuine complaints from initial resistance to change.

Evaluation
The programme should run for one term. Success should be measured using waste per meal served, canteen costs and student satisfaction. If waste falls but students report that portions are inadequate, the system should be adjusted.

Conclusion
Food waste is a sustainability problem that the school can influence directly. The strongest approach is not a single awareness poster but a combination of measurement, flexible portions, better demand planning and student participation. A one-term trial would allow the school to reduce waste while learning which changes are practical for our canteen.

tasks.prompt: Your school is debating whether high-risk outdoor activities should remain part of school trips. Write a text for a school meeting in which you explain educational benefits, address safety and choice, and give a clear recommendation about when such activities are justified.
requirements: Explain educational benefits of challenging outdoor activities.
Address safety, preparation and student choice.
Give a clear recommendation about when the activities are justified.
tasks.audience: Students, teachers and parents at a school meeting
tasks.purpose: Persuade the school community to adopt a balanced approach to risk
tasks.textTypeRationale: A speech fits a school meeting and allows direct engagement with competing concerns before a clear recommendation.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: Benefitsとrisksを両方扱い、最後に条件付きの明確な結論を出しています。Speechとしてaudienceに問いかける形とThank youまで含め、registerとconventionsを合わせています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Good afternoon teachers and students,

Our school is considering whether students should be allowed to take part in high-risk outdoor activities such as climbing, white-water rafting and long-distance expeditions. Some people believe these activities are irresponsible. Others argue that removing all risk also removes valuable opportunities to grow. I believe schools should allow challenging activities, but only when risk is managed seriously.

Why participate at all? Because controlled challenge teaches lessons that are difficult to reproduce in a classroom. On an expedition, students discover that preparation matters. They must communicate, manage tiredness, make decisions and support people who are struggling. Confidence gained from completing something genuinely difficult can be more meaningful than confidence created by being told that everything will be easy.

However, “challenging” must never become a synonym for careless. Schools have a duty of care. Activities should be led by qualified instructors, equipment must meet safety standards, weather and route conditions must be checked, and emergency plans must be clear. Students also need honest information about hazards before they choose whether to participate.

Choice is essential. A student who is uncomfortable with a particular activity should not be pressured into it simply because classmates are excited. Schools should provide alternative challenges that develop similar skills without forcing everyone to accept the same level of physical risk.

Critics may say that even excellent preparation cannot remove all danger. They are correct. Outdoor activity involves uncertainty. Yet daily life also involves risk, and education partly prepares us to judge it. The goal should not be zero risk at any cost; it should be proportionate risk with strong safeguards and clear educational value.

We also need to distinguish useful challenge from thrill-seeking. An activity is educational when students plan, reflect, cooperate and learn from the experience. It is much harder to justify if its main purpose is simply to produce an exciting photograph.

Reflection after the activity is equally important. Students should be asked what decisions they made, which risks they underestimated and how their team responded when plans changed. Without reflection, even an impressive expedition can become just a memory of discomfort or excitement. With reflection, students can connect the experience to wider skills such as leadership, responsibility and resilience. The learning should continue after everyone has taken off the helmet and gone home.

So should schools run high-risk activities? Yes, when the expected benefits are clear, professional standards are high and participation is genuinely voluntary. No, when excitement is valued more than preparation or when students are pushed beyond reasonable limits.

Young people need opportunities to test themselves. The responsible answer is not to remove every difficult experience, but to teach students how preparation, judgement and teamwork allow them to face difficulty intelligently.

Thank you.

tasks.prompt: A local newspaper has published an article claiming that young people are politically disengaged. Write a text in response in which you explain barriers to youth participation, propose ways schools and local government can help, and argue why meaningful participation matters.
requirements: Explain barriers to meaningful youth participation.
Propose actions for schools or local government.
Argue why youth participation matters for democracy.
tasks.purpose: Challenge a public claim and advocate for meaningful youth civic participation
tasks.textTypeRationale: A letter to the editor directly responds to a published public claim and supports a concise but developed argument.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: 新聞記事へのresponseとして冒頭でclaimに反論し、schools/local government/social mediaという複数の観点を展開しています。最後はfuture citizensへの論点に戻して明確に締めています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Dear Editor,

Politicians frequently complain that young people are uninterested in democracy. Yet when teenagers try to participate, they are often told that they are too inexperienced to have serious opinions. We cannot criticize young people for being disengaged while treating their engagement as inconvenient.

Schools should do more than explain how elections work. Students need opportunities to practise civic participation. A lesson about voting is useful, but organizing a debate, writing to a local representative or researching a council decision teaches something different: public decisions are made by people, and ordinary citizens can influence them.

Local governments also have a role. Council meetings and consultation documents are often technically open to everyone but practically inaccessible to teenagers. Meetings may take place during school hours, websites may use complicated language and young people may not know that consultations exist. A youth advisory panel with a clear link to the council could provide a realistic route into local decision-making.

Social media can help, but it should not become the only form of participation. Sharing a campaign post takes seconds and may spread information widely, yet lasting political change usually requires more: checking evidence, listening to opposing views, organizing with others and continuing after the first burst of attention has disappeared.

Some adults worry that encouraging youth participation will bring poorly informed opinions into politics. But poor information is not limited to one age group. The solution is better civic education and stronger habits of verification, not silence. Young people are directly affected by decisions about education, transport, housing and climate policy. They deserve structured opportunities to understand and discuss those choices.

Schools should also expose students to disagreement that is structured and respectful. Civic education becomes shallow if every issue is presented as though there is one obvious correct opinion. Students need practice comparing evidence, recognizing trade-offs and changing their minds when arguments are stronger than expected. That experience can reduce the temptation to treat politics as a battle between teams. Democracy depends not only on having a voice, but on learning how to listen.

Participation also creates responsibility. It is easy to say that “leaders should fix everything.” It is harder, but more useful, to propose a realistic change, hear objections and revise an idea. Those are democratic skills.

Not every teenager will become a political activist, nor should they. Civic participation includes voting, volunteering, joining community organizations, attending meetings, signing petitions and simply staying informed. The goal is not to tell young people what to believe. It is to show them that democracy is something people do, not something that happens somewhere else.

If communities want engaged citizens in the future, they should stop waiting until people turn eighteen to begin treating their voices seriously.

Yours faithfully,
A student citizen

tasks.prompt: Your school wants to introduce students to fair trade as part of a poverty-awareness campaign. Write a text that explains what fair trade can achieve, discusses its limitations, and gives practical advice about how the school community can make informed choices.
requirements: Explain what fair trade aims to achieve.
Discuss limitations rather than presenting it as a complete solution.
Give practical advice for informed school purchasing.
tasks.audience: Students and families in the school community
tasks.purpose: Inform readers and encourage practical, informed action
tasks.textTypeRationale: A brochure works well for awareness campaigns because it can organize short explanatory sections and practical advice for a broad audience.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: Brochureらしくquestion headingsと短いsectionsを使い、読みやすさを優先しています。Fair tradeの利点だけでなくlimitsも示すことで、単純なcampaign messageより深いMessageにしています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Fair Trade: What Your Lunch Can Change

What is fair trade?
Fair trade is an approach to trade that aims to give producers more reliable prices and safer, fairer working conditions. It is commonly associated with products such as coffee, cocoa, tea and bananas, although certification systems differ.

Why does it matter?
Many products pass through long international supply chains. The price paid by a consumer is divided among farmers, processors, transport companies, retailers and others. Producers at the beginning of the chain may have little power to negotiate, especially when prices change suddenly. Low and unstable income can make it difficult for families to pay for food, healthcare or education.

What can fair-trade systems do?
A well-designed scheme can provide minimum-price protection, additional community funding or standards covering working conditions and environmental practices. Producer organizations may also gain stronger bargaining power by working collectively.

Is it a complete solution?
No. A label does not automatically end poverty. Certification can cost money, not every farmer can access the same markets, and higher retail prices do not always mean that all additional money reaches producers. Fair trade should therefore be judged by evidence rather than treated as a perfect ethical guarantee.

What can our school do?
Choose carefully: The canteen can identify products for which credible fair-trade options are available and compare price, quality and supplier information.

Ask questions: Students can investigate who produces common products and how value is distributed through the supply chain.

Avoid waste: Paying more for a responsibly sourced product makes little sense if large amounts are thrown away.

Support informed purchasing: Posters or QR codes in the canteen could explain why selected products were chosen without suggesting that one purchase solves global inequality.

Students can also examine the limits of ethical consumption. A family with a tight budget may not be able to choose the most expensive certified product, and it would be unfair to turn shopping into a test of personal morality. Institutions such as schools and companies often have more purchasing power than individual consumers. That is why collective procurement policies can matter: they shift some responsibility from isolated shoppers to organizations that buy large quantities.

Think beyond shopping
Poverty is influenced by education, healthcare, employment, public policy, conflict and access to resources. Consumer choices are only one part of a much larger picture. However, they can still encourage companies and institutions to make supply chains more transparent.

Our message
A school cannot eliminate global poverty through its lunch menu. It can, however, use everyday purchasing decisions as an opportunity to learn about wages, power and responsibility. Fair trade is most valuable when it begins a conversation rather than ending one.

Ask where products come from. Ask who benefits. Then make a choice with more information than you had before.

tasks.prompt: You visited an exhibition that combines traditional art with works created using generative AI. Write a text in which you evaluate the exhibition, discuss how it handles questions of creativity and authorship, and recommend whether others should visit it.
requirements: Evaluate the exhibition rather than only describe it.
Discuss creativity, authorship or ethical questions raised by AI art.
Give a clear recommendation to potential visitors.
tasks.audience: Readers considering whether to visit the exhibition
tasks.purpose: Evaluate the exhibition and make a recommendation
tasks.textTypeRationale: A review is designed to combine description, evaluation and a recommendation for prospective audiences.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: Reviewなのでstrengths/weaknessesを評価し、最後に読者へのrecommendationを明確にしています。作品内容だけでなく、exhibitionがauthorshipやcopyrightをどう扱うかまで評価している点が展開の深さにつながります。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Review: “Shared Canvas” — When AI Enters the Gallery

The new exhibition Shared Canvas asks a question that sounds simple but becomes more difficult in every room: if a machine helps create an image, who is the artist? Rather than offering one answer, the exhibition places traditional paintings, digitally manipulated photographs and AI-generated works beside one another and lets the tension build.

The strongest section focuses on process. Visitors can see an artist’s original sketches, the text prompts entered into an image generator and several rejected outputs before the final piece. This is important because AI art is often discussed as if a person presses one button and instantly receives a finished masterpiece. The exhibition shows that selection, revision and intention can still matter, even when the tool is unfamiliar.

One installation is particularly effective. A wall displays hundreds of similar machine-generated portraits, while a small screen shows the human artist repeatedly changing instructions about age, expression, lighting and cultural references. The final portrait is not impressive because the software is “creative” in a human sense; it is impressive because the work makes us think about authorship and choice.

The exhibition is weaker when it discusses the ethical questions behind the technology. A short label mentions that AI systems may be trained on enormous collections of existing images, but the issue of artists’ consent and copyright deserves more space. Visitors are asked whether AI can be original, yet they receive less information about where the visual material used to train systems may have come from.

The curators also avoid the easy mistake of presenting technology as either a miracle or a threat. Several conventional artists explain that they use AI for experimentation but complete their final work through painting, photography or sculpture. Others reject it entirely. These conflicting views make the exhibition more interesting.

The exhibition is also accessible to visitors who know little about AI. Interactive displays explain how prompts can be revised and how different outputs emerge, but the explanations avoid pretending that the process is magical. I especially appreciated a station where visitors could compare several results generated from nearly identical instructions. The differences made it clear that the tool contains unpredictability, while the human user still makes decisions about what to keep, reject and present.

Shared Canvas will probably frustrate anyone looking for a final definition of “real art.” That is exactly why I recommend it. The exhibition treats art as an argument about intention, technique, context and interpretation rather than as a list of approved tools.

I left unconvinced that machines are artists, but more convinced that artists will continue to use machines in unexpected ways. If you enjoy exhibitions that make you debate with the person beside you on the way out, Shared Canvas is worth visiting.

tasks.prompt: A close friend has asked how growing up with more than one cultural background has influenced your sense of identity. Write a text in which you explain how your identity changes across contexts, discuss challenges created by other people's expectations, and reflect on what belonging means to you now.
requirements: Explain how identity can shift across contexts.
Discuss challenges created by other people's expectations or stereotypes.
Reflect on what belonging means to you now.
tasks.purpose: Respond personally and reflectively to a question about cultural identity
tasks.textTypeRationale: A personal letter best matches the close relationship and reflective purpose implied by the task.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: Friendへのletterなので、formalな分析ではなく個人的な経験と気持ちを中心にしています。一方でstereotypeやbelongingを具体的に掘り下げ、単なる日記にならないようMessageを展開しています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Dear Mina,

You asked me last week whether I ever feel “half Japanese and half Korean” or whether I feel more connected to one side. I have been thinking about your question because the simplest answer — “both” — is true but not very useful.

My identity changes depending on where I am. In Japan, people sometimes notice the Korean part of my family first, especially when they hear my mother speaking or learn that we visit relatives in Korea. In Korea, the opposite can happen. Suddenly my Japanese school life becomes the unusual part of the story. For years I found that frustrating because I wanted one answer that would make everyone understand me immediately.

Now I think the problem was the assumption that identity has to fit into one box. At home, languages, food and family habits mix naturally. We do not stop to label every tradition before using it. Some things feel Korean, some feel Japanese and some simply feel like our family.

Language has probably shaped this most strongly. Certain feelings are easier to express in one language than another, and jokes do not always survive translation. I used to worry that switching languages made me less “authentic,” but now I see it as an extra way of understanding people. It also makes me notice how differently the same idea can sound depending on tone and context.

There are still awkward moments. Sometimes people expect me to explain an entire country because of my background, as if I represent millions of people. Other times someone makes a stereotype sound like a compliment. I am learning to correct those comments without feeling that I must defend every part of my identity.

I have also realized that other people’s categories can change faster than my own feelings. On school forms I may be asked to choose one nationality, while in conversation someone may ask which language is my “real” language. Those questions are often practical, but they can make a complicated identity look like a problem that needs to be simplified. I am becoming more comfortable answering accurately even when the accurate answer takes more than one word.

The best part is that belonging no longer feels like a competition. I can care about more than one place and still be critical of both. I can inherit traditions and choose which ones matter to me. I can also build new habits that belong to neither side exactly.

So if you ask me again who I am, I will probably still say “both,” but I mean something richer now. I do not feel divided into two equal halves. I feel like one person whose roots grow in more than one direction.

Thanks for asking the question seriously. It helped me find a better answer.

Take care,
Aya

tasks.prompt: Your school has launched a programme to support students who have recently arrived after displacement caused by conflict. Write a text for the school newspaper in which you report what the programme does, include reactions from people involved, and explain challenges that still remain.
requirements: Report the main features of the support programme.
Include reactions or perspectives from people involved.
Explain challenges that still remain.
tasks.purpose: Inform the school community objectively about a new support programme
tasks.textTypeRationale: A news report best fits an informative school-newspaper task requiring facts, reactions and continuing challenges.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: News reportらしくheadline→lead→programme details→quote→remaining challenges→今後の見通しという構成です。Writer自身の感情を前面に出さず、neutral toneを保つことがCriterion Cで重要です。
tasks.modelAnswer:
New Student Programme Welcomes Families Displaced by Conflict

Riverside International School has launched a support programme for students who have recently arrived in the city after displacement caused by armed conflict. The programme combines language support, peer mentoring and practical guidance for families entering a new school system.

According to school staff, the initiative was created after enrolment of newly arrived students increased during the past year. Teachers reported that academic ability was often not the main difficulty. New students also had to understand unfamiliar timetables, technology platforms, assessment methods and social expectations while adjusting to a new language and community.

Each participating student is matched with a trained peer mentor for the first six weeks. Mentors help newcomers locate classrooms, join clubs and understand everyday routines. The school has also introduced weekly language workshops focused on practical classroom communication rather than only formal grammar.

Family support is another part of the programme. Important school documents are now available in several languages, and interpreters can be requested for key meetings. Staff members said this is intended to reduce misunderstandings and allow parents to participate in decisions about their children’s education.

The school has emphasized that students are not required to discuss experiences of conflict. Counsellors are available, but participation is voluntary and teachers have been advised not to ask students for personal stories simply out of curiosity.

Student reactions have been generally positive. One peer mentor said the programme had made her more aware of how many unwritten rules exist in school life. “I thought I was just showing someone around,” she explained. “Then I realized I was explaining things I had never needed to think about.”

Teachers involved in the programme also received guidance on assessment. Newly arrived students may understand course content but need more time to demonstrate that understanding in English. The school is therefore encouraging teachers to distinguish language difficulty from subject knowledge where course rules allow. This does not mean lowering standards. It means making sure that temporary language barriers do not lead staff to underestimate what a student can think, calculate or understand.

Some challenges remain. The number of languages spoken by new families makes translation difficult, and teachers say additional training would help them respond to students with interrupted schooling. The school is seeking partnerships with local community organizations to expand support.

The programme will be reviewed at the end of the academic year using feedback from students, families and teachers. School leaders say the goal is not to create a separate system for displaced students but to make existing education more accessible.

The initiative reflects a broader challenge facing schools in communities receiving refugees and other displaced people: providing immediate practical support while avoiding assumptions about students’ abilities, experiences or identities.

tasks.prompt: Your school is reviewing whether students from different financial backgrounds have equal access to learning opportunities. Write a text for school leaders in which you identify barriers, recommend realistic measures, and explain how progress should be reviewed without stigmatizing students.
requirements: Identify barriers linked to financial inequality.
Recommend realistic measures that improve access.
Explain how progress can be reviewed while protecting dignity.
tasks.purpose: Recommend practical measures to reduce educational inequality
tasks.textTypeRationale: A proposal allows clear identification of barriers, structured recommendations, implementation and review.
tasks.modelAnswerJa: Resources/academic support/costs/information accessという複数のbarrierに対して具体策を対応させています。Proposalらしくimplementationとbenefitsまで示し、単なる意見文ではなくdecision-making用の文書にしています。
tasks.modelAnswer:
Proposal: Reducing Educational Inequality in Our School Community

Objective
This proposal recommends three measures to reduce unequal access to learning opportunities among students whose families have different financial resources.

Issue
Our school offers strong academic and extracurricular opportunities, but participation is not equally easy for everyone. Some activities require paid materials, transport, private devices or additional tutoring. Students may therefore have different chances to benefit from the same school even when formal enrolment is equal.

Recommendation 1: Shared access to essential resources
The school should maintain a discreet lending system for laptops, calculators, art materials and other essential equipment. Access should be based on need without requiring students to repeatedly explain private financial circumstances to individual teachers. A single confidential application process would protect dignity and reduce inconsistency.

Recommendation 2: Academic support inside school
Free peer tutoring and teacher-supported study sessions should be available several times each week. This would not replace professional support for students with specific learning needs, but it would provide an alternative for families who cannot pay for private tutoring. Sessions should be advertised to all students so that attendance is normal rather than stigmatizing.

Recommendation 3: Review participation costs
Before approving trips, clubs or competitions, the school should identify the full cost, including transport, clothing and equipment. Where costs are high, organizers should provide subsidies, shared equipment or lower-cost alternatives. No student should discover after joining that an activity has hidden expenses they cannot meet.

The school should also review information access. Opportunities such as scholarships, competitions and enrichment programmes are sometimes announced through channels that not every family follows closely. A central online page, regular reminders and clear deadlines would make access more consistent. Information should explain financial support openly so students do not assume that an activity is “not for people like me” before asking. Equal opportunity depends partly on whether people know an opportunity exists.

Implementation
A small committee of students, teachers and administrators could audit current barriers during the first term. Anonymous student feedback would be especially useful because some families may be reluctant to discuss financial pressure publicly. The committee should then publish a short action plan and review progress annually.

Benefits
These measures would improve equal access without lowering academic expectations. Students would still be responsible for effort, attendance and meeting course requirements, but financial circumstances would have less influence on whether they can obtain basic tools or additional help.

Conclusion
Educational equality does not mean that every student has identical needs. It means that avoidable barriers should not determine who can participate and progress. A coordinated resource-lending system, free academic support and careful review of participation costs would be realistic first steps toward a school community in which opportunity depends less on family income.
